one_liner: C++20/23 dependency-injection and event-queue framework with HTTP services on Boost.Beast; its 'faster than Beast' numbers come from a broken baseline.
what_it_does: Ichor is a microservice bootstrapping framework: services declare dependencies in their constructors or through a DependencyRegister, and a DependencyManager starts, stops and injects them on a per-thread event queue (Boost.Asio, io_uring, or sd-event backends) with coroutine Tasks. The HTTP server is an optional service: you register routes with hostService->addRoute(HttpMethod::post, "/ping", handler) and return an HttpResponse from a coroutine. It is a different programming model, not a drop-in replacement for a Beast server, and HTTP support is a partial HTTP/1.1 implementation (HTTPS only through the Beast backend).
how_it_is_fast: There is no measured speed technique to credit: the HTTP path of the benchmarked build is Boost.Beast itself (Boost::v1::HttpHostService reads with http::async_read inside Asio stackful coroutines and writes through a per-connection outbox). What Ichor adds is structure: the read loop keeps reading the next request while the route handler runs as a queued event, and the framework runs on mimalloc, ankerl unordered_dense maps and glaze JSON. A non-Beast HTTP host on its own TCP services and an io_uring queue (liburing, Linux) also exist, but no HTTP numbers are published for them.
when_to_use: You want an OSGi-style service lifecycle (dependencies appear and disappear at runtime, dependents are stopped and restarted) plus thread confinement in a C++20/23 codebase, and HTTP is one service among Redis, etcd, timers and TCP.
You prefer coroutine route handlers over hand-written Beast session code and can live with Beast-level or lower throughput.
Linux services that may later move to the io_uring queue without changing service code (the framework's stated goal of swapping submission/completion backends).
Projects that want hardened builds by default (_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3, stack protector, -fno-rtti) and can vendor several submodules.
when_not_to_use: You need a faster HTTP server than Boost.Beast: no valid measurement shows one, and Drogon (about 132k req/s) and Go fasthttp (about 166k req/s) beat Ichor (about 67k-87k req/s) on Ichor's own benchmark page.
Full HTTP/1.1 compliance, HTTP/2 or HTTPS without Boost.Beast: the README calls HTTP support partial.

Large service graphs created at startup: the project's own conclusions say creating services with dependencies is likely O(N^2) and memory-heavy (the multi-threaded start benchmark peaks at about 300 MB).

You want a small dependency footprint or a stable, widely used API: it is a single-maintainer 'personal project' (237 stars, version 0.5.0) that pulls in Boost (context, coroutine, fiber), a forked fmt, a forked static mimalloc, glaze, spdlog, Catch2 and liburing.
macOS production use: support is described as partial (brew llvm, possible ASan false positives with Beast).

integration.form: compiled library built with CMake (add_library without a type, so static unless BUILD_SHARED_LIBS is set; project ichor 0.5.0), with optional service sources selected by CMake flags
integration.dependencies: Boost 1.70+ (context, coroutine, fiber) for the Beast/Asio backend; git submodules fmt (fork), mimalloc (volt-software static fork), glaze, spdlog (optional), Catch2 (tests), liburing (Linux); OpenSSL for HTTPS; hiredis optional
integration.min_toolchain: GCC 12+, Clang 15+ or MSVC 17.4+; CMake 3.22; CMake sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23 on non-Windows although the project describes itself as C++20
integration.platforms: Linux (x86-64, aarch64, musl), Windows; partial macOS; io_uring backend Linux-only; arch tuning presets from X86_64 to AVX-512 and Raspberry Pi
integration.thread_safety: Thread confinement: each DependencyManager and its services live on one event-queue thread; cross-thread communication goes through queued events, and code on threads Ichor does not manage is 'on your own' (README)

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the Beast comparison: benchmarks/beast_benchmark/boost_beast_benchmark.cpp sets keep_alive(true) on the response but then calls shutdown(shutdown_send) and accept(), which closes the socket, after every response, so wrk reconnects for every request (read errors equal the request count in all three runs), while Ichor keeps connections open; each Beast worker also serves one connection at a time, and the worker count used is not stated. At 2 connections Beast's mean latency (20.80 us) beat Ichor's (29.17 us).

The published Ichor runs are stale relative to the code: the top -H output shows separate 'HttpCon' and 'DepMan' threads (the README admits Ichor 'cheats' with an extra thread while Drogon, fasthttp and Beast ran on one), but the current BoostAsioQueue is a single-threaded io_context (BOOST_ASIO_CONCURRENCY_HINT_UNSAFE_IO) since the 'Refactor boost support to proper event loop, removing need for locks and threads' commit; the HTTP section dates from the Dec 2022 to Feb 2024 README revisions.
Run lengths differ (Ichor 60 s, every other server 10 s), and the benchmarks README itself says the numbers identify bottlenecks rather than showcase performance.

In the Beast-backed host, a request without keep-alive gets a keep_alive(false) response, but the server does not close the socket itself; the read loop only ends on end_of_stream, abort, timeout (30 s) or a bad descriptor.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Ichor only for its dependency-injection, lifecycle and thread-confinement model; for raw HTTP throughput over Boost.Beast, aeronet (2.75x on headers, 1.10-1.20x on static and routing at 10 connections) and libevhtp (about 1.15x) have valid comparisons, and Drogon is roughly 1.5-2x faster than Ichor on Ichor's own page.
verified_claims_summary: On an AMD 7950X with Ubuntu 22.04 (gcc 13.1.1 or clang 18, not stated which), wrk POSTed {"sequence": 2} to /ping: Ichor's Beast-backed pong example reached 67,195 / 87,049 / 72,972 req/s at 2 / 400 / 20,000 connections against 41,397 / 73,975 / 37,311 req/s for a 'pure Beast' server that closes the connection after every response. The 1.18x-1.96x gap therefore measures per-request TCP reconnects (and, in the old architecture, an extra handler thread), not a faster HTTP stack; there is no valid evidence that Ichor beats Beast.
status_note: Active single-maintainer MIT project (last commits 2026-02-06, no open issues), copyable and well hardened by default, but its HTTP numbers come from a crippled baseline on a 2022-2024 architecture that has since been rewritten, so treat it as a DI and lifecycle framework rather than a fast HTTP server.
